predictions.title: Open-weight text-diffusion LLMs add a second family or edge runtime by Q1 2027
predictions.body: Google's June 10 release of DiffusionGemma under Apache 2.0 is the moment open-weight text diffusion stopped being a research curiosity and shipped as a usable local model: a 26B Mixture-of-Experts (3.8B active) built on the Gemma 4 backbone with an added diffusion head, it abandons left-to-right autoregressive decoding to refine a 256-token block in parallel over multiple passes, locking in confident tokens as context for up to 4x faster generation, and it lands with native support across vLLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, NVIDIA NeMo, and Unsloth, plus a shipped Unsloth Sudoku fine-tune that exploits its bidirectional attention. Two things make this a seed rather than a one-off. First, Google is explicit that output quality trails standard autoregressive Gemma 4 and steers production work back to the autoregressive model, positioning diffusion squarely for speed-critical, low-concurrency local inference - the exact envelope an edge runtime is built to fill. Second, the on-device stack is not yet ready for it: llama.cpp support is listed only as coming, so the GGUF/CPU path where Gemma-class weights are actually deployed locally cannot run block-parallel diffusion decoding on launch day, and the open-weight text-diffusion field has exactly one member. The forward thesis is that text diffusion hardens into an established open-weight model category rather than remaining a single Google checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 EITHER a second independent major open-weight text-diffusion language model ships with its own model card and weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher (the strongest candidates being Alibaba/Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral, or NVIDIA), OR a mainstream on-device inference runtime that did not support it at DiffusionGemma's launch - llama.cpp foremost, or LM Studio, Ollama, or MLX as a packaged GGUF/edge path - ships first-class block-parallel text-diffusion decoding so the format runs on the consumer CPU/edge stack. A research-only paper with no released weights, a one-off Google follow-up checkpoint, or a runtime that merely wraps the existing PyTorch path without native diffusion-decoding support does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LLM release or genuine edge-runtime support for the decoding scheme. If by March 31, 2027 DiffusionGemma is still the only open-weight text-diffusion model and no mainstream on-device runtime has added native diffusion decoding, the prediction fails.

reasoning.because: DiffusionGemma shipped June 10 as the first open-weight text-diffusion LLM; no llama.cpp support yet
reasoning.given: diffusion's 4x-faster low-concurrency profile fits the edge, but the GGUF/CPU stack can't run it yet
reasoning.so_that: a second open-weight diffusion LLM ships, or a mainstream on-device runtime adds native diffusion decoding
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027: a second open-weight diffusion LLM, or on-device diffusion decoding
reasoning.plain_language: Google made the first open AI that writes in parallel, not word by word; soon a rival copies it or local apps run it.

predictions.summary: The June 10 DiffusionGemma is the first major open-weight text-diffusion LLM, decoding 256-token blocks in parallel for up to 4x faster output, but llama.cpp support is only coming. Expect text diffusion to form an open-weight category by Q1 2027 via a second release or on-device runtime support.

predictions.title: Durable ask-user checkpoints become a standard harness primitive by H1 2027
predictions.body: Simon Willison's datasette-agent 0.2a0, released June 10, adds a capability most autonomous-loop harnesses still lack: a tool that declares a context parameter receives a ToolContext object and can call await context.ask_user(...) to suspend the run and ask the operator a yes/no, multiple-choice, or free-text question instead of guessing, and the suspended conversation persists to the database and survives a server restart, so the half-finished run resumes once the human answers; a paired save_query tool writes agent-generated SQL as a stored query only after explicit human approval. This matters because it is not a UI confirmation popup but a durable, restart-surviving suspend/resume checkpoint implemented at the individual-tool level, which is exactly the human-in-the-loop primitive that durable-execution agent frameworks have been converging toward from the orchestration side. As agents move from chat into long-running unattended work, the failure mode shifts from a wrong answer to a wrong irreversible action taken with no chance to intervene, and the durable answer is to let any tool pause the loop, ask a question, and hold its state across process death until a person responds - a control surface that does not exist if the only checkpoints are ephemeral in-memory prompts that vanish on restart. The forward thesis is that this ask-user-and-survive-restart checkpoint hardens from a single open-source implementation into an expected, named feature of the major agent harnesses and coding-agent runtimes. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by H1 2027 at least two major agent harnesses or coding-agent frameworks (the strongest candidates being a Claude Code / Codex CLI / Cursor / Cline-class coding agent, an orchestration framework such as LangGraph or a durable-execution runtime like Temporal or Restate, or a managed agent platform like AWS Bedrock AgentCore or Microsoft Foundry) ship a documented mid-execution human-input primitive in which a running tool can suspend the agent, request a typed answer or approval from the operator, and resume the same run after a full process or server restart - state persisted, not re-prompted from scratch. A transient in-memory approval prompt, a pre-run permission allowlist, or an after-the-fact audit log does not count; the marker is a documented suspend-ask-resume checkpoint that durably survives restart, shipped by a non-Datasette stack.

reasoning.because: datasette-agent ToolContext.ask_user pauses a run to ask the operator; paused state survives restart
reasoning.given: long-running agents need durable human-in-the-loop checkpoints, not prompts that vanish on restart
reasoning.so_that: two-plus major harnesses ship a documented suspend-ask-resume human-input primitive that survives restart
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; two-plus non-Datasette harnesses ship a restart-durable checkpoint
reasoning.plain_language: An open-source AI agent can pause, ask the human, and resume after a restart; big agent tools will copy it.

predictions.summary: datasette-agent 0.2 lets any tool suspend an agent run to ask the operator a question, with the paused conversation persisted so it survives a server restart and resumes once answered. Expect this durable checkpoint to become a standard primitive in two-plus major agent harnesses by H1 2027.

predictions.title: Intel Foundry lands a second external AI-chip customer on 18A by Q2 2027
predictions.body: The semiconductor tape's June 8 snap-back - Intel up about 8.5% and Micron about 9% reversing the prior Friday's roughly $1 trillion Broadcom-driven washout - was led not by GPU-demand names but by two US-manufacturing catalysts: reporting that Alphabet had tapped Intel to manufacture about 3 million in-house chips, and that Nvidia was evaluating Intel's 18A process for future parts. The signal that matters is not the one-day price move but who carried it - the market rotated leadership from the merchant-GPU vendors that led the prior run toward domestic foundry capacity, repricing Intel specifically as a contract manufacturer for other companies' custom AI silicon rather than only as a struggling CPU vendor. A single hyperscaler engagement plus one fabless evaluation does not yet establish Intel Foundry as a credible second-source merchant fab for leading-edge AI parts; it could remain a one-off in-house Alphabet job and an evaluation that never converts. The forward thesis is that the Alphabet 18A signal hardens into an external-customer franchise: by Q2 2027 at least one additional named hyperscaler or fabless AI-chip designer beyond the initial Alphabet engagement publicly commits to manufacturing a leading-edge AI accelerator, custom inference ASIC, or networking part on an Intel Foundry advanced node (18A or its 14A successor) - confirmed via an on-record customer announcement, a signed foundry agreement, a tape-out disclosure, or an executive statement naming the part - with Nvidia's reported 18A evaluation the leading candidate to convert. The marker is a committed external leading-edge customer for a named AI part, not a packaging-only deal, a memorandum of intent, or further unconfirmed evaluation reporting. The counter-risk is that 18A yield or schedule slips and the prospective customers stay with TSMC for leading-edge AI volume, leaving Intel's external book limited to the in-house Alphabet work and trailing-edge fill.

reasoning.because: June 8: Alphabet tapped Intel to make ~3M in-house chips; Nvidia evaluating Intel 18A; INTC +8.5%
reasoning.given: the chip rebound rotated leadership to domestic foundry capacity, repricing Intel as a merchant fab
reasoning.so_that: a second named hyperscaler or fabless designer commits a leading-edge AI part to an Intel Foundry node
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; >=1 external Intel-Foundry 18A/14A AI-chip customer beyond Alphabet
reasoning.plain_language: After Alphabet hired Intel to build its chips and Nvidia started testing Intel's factory, another big chip buyer will likely sign on too.

predictions.summary: Intel's June 8 rebound ran on US-manufacturing catalysts - Alphabet tapping Intel to make ~3M in-house chips and Nvidia evaluating its 18A process - repricing Intel as a merchant fab for custom AI silicon. Expect Intel Foundry to win a second named external leading-edge AI-chip customer by Q2 2027.
